children: By Caroline Valetkevitch
U.S. Treasury yields fell on Thursday as oil prices eased and investors digested Wednesday's Federal Reserve interest rate increase and the U.S. central bank's signals for more rate increases ahead.
Oil prices were sharply lower following reports of additional Saudi crude cargoes through Oman that eased supply concerns.
Spikes in oil prices tied to the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran have driven concerns about inflation and boosted yields recently.

Yields mostly rose on Wednesday after the U.S. central bank raised rates for the first time since 2023 in a widely expected move to try to control persistently higher inflation and as Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh delivered mostly hawkish comments.
Investors were still digesting the Fed's news by Thursday, with much uncertainty remaining over how far the central bank will raise rates to keep inflation in check.

"At first you saw rates rise, now you're seeing a little bit of a giveback of yesterday, but I don't think the market has truly figured out what's going on here," said Ron Albahary, chief investment officer at LNW in Philadelphia.
Traders see a roughly 51% chance of another increase when the central bank next meets in October, according to CME FedWatch.
Overseas, the Bank of England on Thursday held UK rates steady but sounded the alarm on inflation.
UNEMPLOYMENT CLAIMS DROP
Yields held declines after data showing the number of Americans filing claims for unemployment benefits unexpectedly fell last week.

Initial claims for state unemployment benefits dropped 10,000 to a seasonally adjusted 196,000 for the week ended September 12, the Labor Department said on Thursday. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast 208,000 claims for the latest week. The surprise drop likely reflected volatility around last week's Labor Day holiday. Claims are difficult to adjust for seasonal fluctuations around moving public holidays.
A separate report showed U.S. single-family homebuilding increased in August, but a drop in permits for future construction suggested the improvement was likely temporary.
BENCHMARK 10-YEAR YIELD BELOW 5%
The 10-year Treasury yield
, which rose above 5.00% earlier this week for the first time since 2023, was last down 5.7 basis points at 4.947%. The yield on the 30-year bond (US30YT=RR) fell 4.7 basis points to 5.301%.

A closely watched part of the U.S. Treasury yield curve measuring the gap between yields on two- and 10-year Treasury notes (US2US10=TWEB), seen as an indicator of economic expectations, was at a positive 26.6 basis points.
The two-year (US2YT=RR) U.S. Treasury yield, which typically moves in step with interest rate expectations for the Fed, was down 4.8 basis points at 4.679%.
The breakeven rate on five-year U.S. Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS) (US5YTIP=TWEB) was last at 2.322% after closing at 2.353% on September 16.
The 10-year TIPS breakeven rate (US10YTIP=TWEB) was last at 2.305%, indicating the market sees inflation averaging about 2.3% a year for the next decade.
